results.content: Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling (opens in a new tab)Multilevel Mediation (opens in a new tab)Multilevel SEM (opens in a new tab). Three new alternative approaches are proposed for fitting 3-level mediation models using single- and multilevel SEM, and each method is demonstrated with simulated data. Multilevel modeling (MLM) is a popular way of assessing mediation effects with clustered data. ### Analyzing Multilevel Mediation Using Multilevel Structural Equation Models. ### Structural multilevel models for longitudinal mediation analysis: a definition variable approach. ### A Comparison of Multilevel Mediation Modeling Methods: Recommendations for Applied Researchers. This article presents two numerical examples that use simulated data based on published studies in adolescence research to demonstrate how to specify, estimate, and interpret the results of single-level and multilevel mediation analyses to answer key research questions. Traditional approaches for analyzing mediation in nested data are reviewed, multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM) is described as a versatile technique for assessing mediation in fully nested data and two new MSEM-PN specifications are introduced. ### Mediation from Multilevel to Structural Equation Modeling. Multilevel structural equation modeling (SEM) for mediation analysis of longitudinal data provides an ideal approach for several reasons, including the ability to assess effects at different levels of analysis, incorporation of measurement error and possible random effects that vary across individuals. ### Multilevel Mediation With Small Samples: A Cautionary Note on the Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling Framework. It is demonstrated that a broad class of MLMs may be estimated as structural equation models (SEMs), and within the SEM approach it is possible to include measurement models for predictors or outcomes, and to estimate the mediational pathways among predictors explicitly, tasks which are currently difficult with the conventional approach to multilevel modeling. ### Multilevel Modeling of Individual and Group Level Mediated Effects. Multilevel mediational modeling methods were also applied to data from a preventive intervention designed to reduce intentions to use steroids among players on high school football teams and shows how the multilevel technique may lead to more accurate results. ### Lower Level Mediation in Multilevel Models. ### Multilevel Mediation Modeling in Group-Based Intervention Studies. These methods were applied to data from an existing substance use intervention to show the impact multilevel mediation modeling can have on the conclusions drawn from real-world evaluation studies.

results.title: School climate and the socioeconomic literacy achievement gap: Multilevel analysis of compensation, mediation, and moderation models - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: School climate and the socioeconomic literacy achievement gap: Multilevel analysis of compensation, mediation, and moderation models - ScienceDirect
Using a nationally representative sample of fifth- and eighth-grade students in Israel (*N* = 53,801), this study carefully tested whether schools’ positive social climate could compensate for the negative contribution of poor SES background to literacy scores, mediate the SES–test scores association, or moderate the strength of the association between SES and achievement. Poverty and privilege are closely associated with students’ education, particularly literacy skills and reading abilities, to the detriment of children and schools of lower socioeconomic status (SES; Buckingham et al., 2013, Molfese et al., 2003, Neuman and Celano, 2015, OECD, 2020, Sherblom et al., 2006). Despite mounting evidence of higher academic achievement garnered by students experiencing positive climate, the scientific evidence establishing associations among SES background, school climate, and academic achievement has been diverse, suggesting different patterns of influences (Benbenishty et al., 2016, Berkowitz et al., 2017). The absence of a solid theoretical foundation of the mechanism by which positive climate contributes to academics may pose obstacles for school social workers, educators, and policy advocates straining to enhance underprivileged students’ outcomes and catalyze greater equity through more safe and inclusive learning environments. Drawing from ecological systems theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1994), school social work, psychology, and education researchers articulated schools at the center of a larger ecological system in which they are situated and emphasized the reciprocal effects of the school and its multiple contexts that influence students’ outcomes (Bowen et al., 2008, Espelage and Swearer, 2004, Rudasill et al., 2018). Students’ social, emotional, and academic outcomes are shaped by interactions among the within-school context (e.g., school climate, organizational structure), student body, family demographics and characteristics, neighborhood, broader community, educational policy, culture, and ethnic environment (Astor & Benbenishty, 2019). Some argued that a positive school climate could add to student achievement and compensate for the negative contribution of low SES to academics (e.g., O’Malley et al., 2015). Students in the Hebrew language religious public schools typically come from lower SES backgrounds, and their academic achievements are significantly lower than their Hebrew language secular counterparts (Endeweld et al., 2019, National Authority for Measurement and Evaluation in Education, 2020). Her research focuses on school climate and the relationships to students' social, emotional and academic outcomes, the academic, achievement gap, school violence and bullying, teachers' workplace victimization, and schools as learning organizations.
